previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with a history of Addison’s disease, hypothyroidism, hypertension, and microscopic colitis, was readmitted one week after prior discharge due to recurrent nausea, vomiting, and persistent watery diarrhea. She had recently increased her Florinef dose without symptom relief and developed an adrenal crisis, likely exacerbated by malabsorption from chronic diarrhea. In the ED, she received IV hydrocortisone and was stabilized. Labs showed hyponatremia and hyperkalemia, consistent with adrenal insufficiency. She improved with IV fluids and stress-dose steroids, with resolution of nausea and vomiting. Abdominal ultrasound was normal, and stool studies were negative for infection. She remained on home medications including prednisone, Florinef, levothyroxine, and metoprolol. The chronic diarrhea was attributed to microscopic colitis, and outpatient GI follow-up was arranged. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue current medications, maintain a high-salt diet, and seek care if symptoms recurred.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year-old female with ___ disease admitted with nausea, 
lightheadedness, and increased salt craving in setting of 
hyperkalemia.

1. Nausea:  Resolved on arrival to the floor after receiving IVF 
and hydrocortisone 100mg IV x1 in the emergency department. 
Patient reported her symptoms of nausea malaise were very 
similar to those during episodes of mild adrenal crisis in the 
past. Hyperkalemia, lightheadedness, and salt craving were 
consistent with this.  decreased aldosterone. Other etiologies 
considered included gastritis given chronic steroid use, 
pancreatitis, hepatitis, cholecystitis. Patient was on a PPI and 
guaiac negative in the emergency department, had a high normal 
lipase, had normal LFTs, and had no indication of cholecystitis 
or appendicitis on exam. She was continued on her home PPI, 
written for antiemetics although did not require them, and given 
an increased dose of fludrocortisone, as below. On discharge, 
patient was tolerating regular diet without problem.

2. Hyperkalemia:  Patient with potassium 5.7 in outpatient 
clinic on day prior to admission. In the emergency department, 
potassium was 5.5. This was likely related to aldosterone 
deficiency. EKG with peaked T waves, and patient was hydrated in 
the emergency department. On admission, she was given Kayexelate 
30gm PO x1. Repeat EKG was essentially unchanged. She was 
monitored on telemetry. On the morning of discharge, her 
potassium was 3.9 and EKG changes had resolved. As below, 
fludrocortisone dosing was increased.

3. ___ disease:  Patient had many manifestations of 
primary adrenal insufficiency, including hyperpigmentation of 
skin, abdominal pain, salt craving, hyperkalemia. Patient was 
not orthostatic on exam (although this was after she was 
hydrated in the emergency department). Cause of the mild adrenal 
crisis is not known. Patient had recently been downtitrated on 
her prednisone dose; this may have been a contributor. Her 
fludrocortisone dose was increased to 0.2mg PO daily. She was 
continued on prednisone 5mg PO daily.

4. Anemia: Baseline hematocrit ___ 31.5 on admission. MCV 
borderline high at 96. B12, folate checked recently (within past 
6 months) and within normal range. Iron studies checked ___ 
and patient found to be borderline iron deficient (Fe/TIBC < 
15%). Patient may benefit from iron therapy.

5. Hypertension:  Continued metoprolol succinate 25mg PO daily 
per home regimen.

6. Hypothyroidism:  TSH checked ___ was 1.7. She was 
continued on synthroid per home regimen.

7. Depression/anxiety:  Continued citalopram and clonazepam per 
home regimen.

8. Urinary tract infection:  Noted on review of urine culture at 
time of this dictation. Patient will be contacted for treatment 
for uncomplicated urinary tract infection.
